strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: moving beyond pairwise representation alignment to multi-way ($M \ge 3$) alignment, reducing map complexity from $O(M^2)$ to $O(M)$ while ensuring composability and cycle consistency.

The analysis of the trade-off between geometric preservation (GPA) and agreement maximization (GCCA) is insightful and provides clear conceptual motivation for the proposed Geometry-Corrected Procrustes Alignment (GCPA).

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation spanning multiple modalities and tasks: vision stitching under distribution shift, intent clustering on MASSIVE, cross-lingual sentence retrieval on TED-MULTI, person Re-ID on MARKET-1501, and cross-modal retrieval across image, text, and audio on Flickr8k/Flickr30k.

Thorough ablation studies and practical analyses, including incremental universe expansion (GPA-ADD), sensitivity to correspondence noise, hyperparameter sweeps on drift/trust parameters, and candid discussion of failure modes when consensus signal is weak.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is somewhat modest: GPA and GCCA are established classical techniques, and GCPA fundamentally consists of training a lightweight shared residual MLP to nudge GPA universe vectors toward the cross-model mean direction subject to an angular margin constraint.

The theoretical contributions (Propositions 3.1 and 3.2, Theorem B.1) largely reformulate standard properties of multi-set CCA and elementary vector norm identities rather than providing deep theoretical guarantees for the non-linear GCPA stage.

The introduction of the non-linear corrector $T_\theta$ inherently breaks exact orthogonal cycle consistency and isometric guarantees, meaning that the theoretical guarantees motivating the GPA scaffold do not strictly carry over to the final GCPA representations.

The requirement of aligned sample correspondences across all $M$ models during training remains a practical constraint, limiting direct deployment in unpaired or partially observed multi-model ecosystems.

strengths: Relevant and timely problem formulation: Moving from pairwise O(M^2) alignment to a multi-model shared universe (O(M)) is an important practical direction as foundation models proliferate.

Insightful trade-off analysis: The paper clearly identifies the tension between isometric preservation (GPA, ideal for preserving internal topology in stitching/probing) and correlation/agreement maximization (GCCA, which deforms spaces for retrieval), motivating the two-stage GCPA approach.

Comprehensive and diverse empirical evaluation: Experiments span cross-model probing (CIFAR-100), intent clustering (MASSIVE across 10 multilingual models), multilingual sentence retrieval (TED-MULTI), cross-camera person re-ID (MARKET-1501), and multimodal retrieval (FLICKR8K, FLICKR30K across audio, text, and image encoders).

Thorough diagnostics and robustness experiments: The appendix provides valuable analyses, including sensitivity to the trust-region parameters (tau, lambda), stability under correspondence noise and test-time feature noise, continual sequential model addition, and spectral analyses of the corrected universe.

Demonstration of the 'geometric hub' effect: The experiment showing that routing alignment between two fragile/corrupted models through an M-way universe of robust anchor models strengthens weak pairwise links is conceptually compelling.
weaknesses: Relaxation of cycle consistency and invertibility in GCPA: A primary motivation for universe factorization in Section 3.1 is exact cycle consistency and transitivity. However, GCPA introduces a non-linear, non-orthogonal MLP correction T_theta without an explicit inverse. As noted in Appendix D, round-trip mapping and strict cycle consistency no longer hold after the non-linear correction, weakening one of the core theoretical arguments motivating universe alignment over direct mappings.

Added complexity over closed-form GCCA: While GCCA provides an exact closed-form spectral solution (Theorem B.1), GCPA requires a two-stage pipeline involving iterative GPA followed by neural network training with trust-region hyperparameters (tau, lambda). In several retrieval benchmarks (e.g., Table 2 at M=3, Table 8 on FLICKR30K), the performance margins over GCCA are modest.

Complication in incremental addition for GCPA: In GPA, extending the universe to a new model XM+1 is purely modular (solving one orthogonal Procrustes problem against a fixed U). For GCPA, Table 6 shows that simply projecting the new model through the fixed corrector (GCPA-ADD) degrades performance, requiring re-training of the correction module (GCPA-ADD-LIGHT) on all universe representations.

Strong requirement for full multi-way paired correspondences: The methodology assumes matched samples across all M spaces (Xm in R^{N x d}). In practical multi-model ecosystems, full M-way intersection of data is rarely available, and the paper does not explore partially overlapping or unaligned correspondence regimes.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: shifting from quadratic pairwise alignment ($O(M^2)$) to a linear multi-way universe formulation ($O(M)$) that encourages cycle consistency across multiple pretrained representations.

Provides a clear conceptual and mathematical motivation: rigorously contrasting isometric alignment (GPA) which preserves internal geometry with agreement-maximizing alignment (GCCA) which excels at retrieval, and proposing GCPA to balance both objectives.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across multiple domains and modalities, including vision-only probing on CIFAR-100, intent clustering on MASSIVE, multilingual sentence retrieval on TED-MULTI, cross-camera Re-ID on MARKET-1501, and multimodal retrieval on FLICKR8K/FLICKR30K.

Thorough analysis of practical system properties: includes incremental model addition (GPA-ADD and GCPA-ADD), robustness to correspondence noise, computational complexity, and explicit investigations into when consensus corrections degrade.
weaknesses: Loss of strict cycle consistency and isometry post-correction: while the GPA scaffold enforces exact cycle consistency and isometry, the introduction of the non-linear correction $T_\theta$ in GCPA relaxes these guarantees, a trade-off that is noted in the appendix but deserves clearer discussion in the main text.

Reliance on fully matched multi-way correspondence tuples: fitting the consensus direction requires aligned sample instances across all $M$ spaces during training, which can become restrictive when scaling to many heterogeneous models where complete multi-way intersections may be scarce.
Modest performance margins over GCCA on certain retrieval benchmarks (e.g., Table 2 on TED-MULTI), though GCPA demonstrates clearer advantages on multimodal and cross-camera tasks.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: representation alignment research is overwhelmingly focused on pairwise (M=2) setups, which scale quadratically and suffer from transitivity/path inconsistency. Formulating multi-way representation alignment through a shared universe is well-motivated.

Provides a clear and insightful conceptualization of the trade-off between geometric preservation (GPA, necessary for preserving within-model geometry and stitching) and correlation/agreement maximization (GCCA, which deforms space to maximize retrieval performance).

The proposed Geometry-Corrected Procrustes Alignment (GCPA) is intuitive and effective: anchoring to an isometric GPA scaffold while learning a trust-region-regularized consensus correction yields consistent empirical gains across retrieval, clustering, and multimodal alignment.

Extensive experimental validation spanning various domains (inter-architecture vision models on CIFAR-100, 10-language sentence retrieval on TED-Multi, cross-camera person Re-ID on Market-1501, cross-modal retrieval on Flickr8k, and clustering on MASSIVE) alongside informative stress-tests like correspondence noise.
weaknesses: Tension regarding cycle consistency: The paper strongly motivates universe alignment by asserting that it 'guarantees cycle consistency by design' (Section 3.1) and eliminates path dependence. However, because GCPA applies a non-linear MLP $T_\theta$ followed by an asymmetric linear projection back to target space ($u \Omega_n^\top$, Eq. 14), cycle consistency and exact invertibility no longer strictly hold. While acknowledged in Appendix E, this trade-off should be prominently discussed in the main text.

Modest theoretical novelty: The theoretical components (Theorem B.1 and Proposition 3.2) are largely direct algebraic expansions of classical properties of GCCA and cosine/vector sums rather than novel theoretical insights.

Unclear incremental addition for GCPA: In Section 4.2.2, the paper demonstrates that a new model can be efficiently added to an existing universe (GPA-ADD) without retraining the base models. However, this experiment is only conducted for linear GPA. The authors do not clarify or evaluate how a new model is integrated into a trained GCPA universe (e.g., whether $T_\theta$ generalizes zero-shot to $\Omega_{M+1}$, or whether $T_\theta$ must be fine-tuned/refit).

Lack of wall-clock time and memory benchmarking: While theoretical asymptotic complexity ($O(M)$ vs $O(M^2)$) is discussed, empirical execution times across the multi-view alternating GPA iterations, GCCA SVD, and GCPA neural network optimization are omitted.

strengths: Addresses a timely and important problem: moving from pairwise ($O(M^2)$) alignment to multi-way ($O(M)$) alignment across collections of deep representations while maintaining cycle consistency.
Provides a clear conceptual framing of the trade-off between geometric preservation (GPA) for probing/stitching and correlation/agreement maximization (GCCA) for retrieval.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple domains, including vision (CIFAR-100, Market-1501), multilingual NLP (MASSIVE, TED-MULTI), and multimodal representation alignment (Flickr8k with text, image, and audio).
The proposed GCPA formulation is simple, computationally lightweight, and empirically effective at improving any-to-any retrieval and clustering quality over both GPA and linear GCCA.
weaknesses: Potential confounding factor in comparison with GCCA: GCPA uses a non-linear neural network ($T_\theta$, a small MLP) on top of the GPA coordinates, whereas GCCA is strictly linear. It remains unclear whether GCPA's retrieval gains stem primarily from the GPA + consensus scaffold or simply from having non-linear parametric capacity (e.g., Deep GCCA / non-linear multi-view alignment baselines are absent).

Tension with the 'best of both worlds' claim regarding geometric fidelity: One of the core arguments for GPA is that orthogonal transformations preserve internal distances and cycle consistency. However, applying the non-linear map $T_\theta$ in GCPA relaxes strict isometry and breaks exact cycle consistency (as acknowledged in Appendix E). While Appendix C.2 measures drift, the main paper lacks an extensive evaluation of GCPA on standard, uncorrupted cross-model stitching/probing benchmarks (e.g., in Section 4.2.2, only GPA is evaluated).

Strong dependence on multi-way aligned paired data: The consensus target $c_i$ requires co-indexed matched representations across spaces during training. Discussion or analysis of how GCPA behaves when sample correspondences are partially missing across subsets of models is limited.
Methodological novelty is relatively modest, combining classical Generalized Procrustes Analysis with a post-hoc residual MLP nudging vectors toward their centroid with a trust-region cosine loss.

strengths: Clear formulation and motivation: Moving beyond pairwise representation alignment to an M-way universe factorization is timely and practically important, reducing mapping complexity from O(M^2) to O(M) and naturally addressing cycle consistency.

Insightful analysis of the geometry vs. retrieval trade-off: The paper nicely articulates and demonstrates the tension between strict isometry (GPA, which preserves internal geometric structure vital for stitching) and agreement maximization (GCCA, which deforms geometry to optimize cross-model correlation for retrieval).

Effective proposed method (GCPA): The two-stage design—using GPA as an orthogonal geometric scaffold followed by a consensus-guided non-linear correction with a trust-region penalty—is conceptually neat and grounded by Proposition 3.2.

Broad and diverse empirical validation: The experimental evaluation spans a wide variety of domains and tasks, including cross-architecture model stitching on CIFAR-100, multilingual sentence retrieval across 10 languages on TED-MULTI, intent clustering on MASSIVE, cross-camera re-identification on Market-1501, and cross-modal retrieval across image/text/audio on Flickr8k.

Practical utility of incremental addition: Section 4.2.2 convincingly shows that adding a new model to an existing universe (GPA-ADD) requires learning only a single orthogonal map while maintaining competitive transfer performance, avoiding expensive full refitting.
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison between non-linear GCPA and linear baselines: GCPA introduces a non-linear neural network corrector (a multi-layer perceptron T_theta), whereas the primary multi-view baselines compared (GPA, GCCA, PW Procrustes) are purely linear/orthogonal. It is unclear how much of GCPA's retrieval and clustering gains stem from non-linear capacity versus the consensus/trust-region formulation itself. A comparison against non-linear multi-view alignment baselines (e.g., Deep GCCA or non-linear multi-view CCA) is missing.

Asymmetry and loss of invertibility / strict cycle consistency: While GPA guarantees exact invertibility and cycle consistency through orthogonal maps, GCPA applies a non-linear map T_theta only when mapping into the universe (toU), but defines fromU simply as multiplication by Omega_n^T. Because T_theta is not an invertible orthogonal transformation, round-trip mappings (m -> universe -> m) and multi-hop compositions no longer preserve strict cycle consistency or exact metric topology.

Strict requirement of full cross-modal correspondences during training: The formulation assumes paired instances across all M representation spaces simultaneously (or a shared index set). In large-scale real-world setups with M >= 3 modalities or models, complete multi-way aligned tuples are often difficult to obtain compared to partial pairwise overlaps.

Modest technical novelty: The individual components—Generalized Procrustes Analysis, Generalized CCA, and training a small MLP against the sample mean vector with a hinge/slack penalty—are largely standard classical tools; the primary contribution lies in their synthesis and empirical exploration within modern deep representation spaces.
